content: How does a B-tree index actually reduce the work for an equality lookup? I understand that it narrows the rows by key, but I sometimes picture that as almost constant time regardless of table size.

A B-tree follows a short path from the root through internal pages to a leaf containing the key. That is logarithmic, not constant, although the tree is usually shallow enough to feel constant in practice. After finding the leaf entry, the database may still fetch matching table rows, so duplicate values, random I/O, and cache state can dominate the traversal cost.
When does the number of matching rows become large enough that the optimizer stops using the index? Is there a standard selectivity percentage where a sequential scan becomes cheaper?

There is no universal percentage. The crossover depends on row width, clustering, storage speed, cached pages, and the cost settings used by the optimizer. Fetching many scattered table pages through an index can cost more than reading the table once in order. Estimates around a few percent are common rules of thumb, but an actual plan can switch much earlier or later.
Does that mean a range condition is basically several equality lookups joined together, or can the leaf pages be walked continuously once the first boundary has been found?

A range scan normally descends the tree once to locate the lower boundary, then walks linked or logically adjacent leaf entries until the upper boundary is reached. It is not repeated root-to-leaf lookup for every value. Performance is especially good when the required table rows follow a similar physical order; otherwise, leaf scanning may still trigger scattered heap reads.
How does caching change that crossover? If the entire index fits in memory but the table does not, I would expect the indexed plan to stay favorable for much broader ranges.

Keeping the index resident removes most index-page I/O, but it does not remove the cost of fetching table pages. A broad range can touch nearly every table page even through a cached index. The indexed plan remains attractive longer when qualifying rows are clustered or the query is covered by the index; for scattered rows, the table scan may still win surprisingly early.

With a composite index on customer_id, status, and created_at, how does the column order control which filters are fast? I know the leftmost columns get priority, but that description feels incomplete.

The entries are sorted lexicographically: first by customer_id, then status within each customer, then created_at within each pair. Equality conditions on a leading sequence let the engine reach a narrow contiguous region. Once a leading column is missing, later columns usually cannot define one clean range, although some engines can use skip scans, filtering, or bitmap operations.
Suppose the query fixes customer_id and uses a created_at range but does not mention status. Does status block the range scan completely, or does the engine scan each status bucket?

In the ordinary access pattern, the engine finds the portion for that customer and scans across every status, applying the created_at condition as a filter. It cannot treat all matching dates as one contiguous interval because each status restarts the date ordering. Some optimizers can probe each distinct status value, but that depends on engine support and cardinality.
When would created_at belong before status in practice, given that status has fewer distinct values and should divide the index into a smaller number of sections?

Distinct-count alone does not decide column order. Put columns according to recurring predicates and ordering needs. If queries usually fix customer_id, constrain a date range, and merely filter status, placing created_at second often gives a tighter range scan. If they usually fix both customer and status before ranging over dates, the original order aligns better with the workload.
How does ORDER BY created_at affect that choice? I assume the index can provide the order whenever created_at appears anywhere in the key, even if status is between it and customer_id.

The intervening column matters. With customer_id fixed but status unconstrained, the original index produces separate date-ordered runs for each status, not one globally date-ordered stream. A final sort or merge may still be required. If both customer_id and status are fixed, created_at becomes the next varying key and the index can directly supply its order.
Would two indexes with the last two columns reversed be reasonable, or is that usually redundant enough that one should be selected as the general version?

They support meaningfully different access patterns, so they are not logically redundant. Whether both are worthwhile depends on query frequency, latency targets, write volume, and storage. Compare representative plans and measure total workload cost. Often one ordering handles the dominant path while a smaller specialized or partial index covers the important exception.

When does adding selected output columns to an index turn a lookup into an index-only scan? I understand the index must cover the query, but does it effectively contain a small copy of the table rows?

A covering index contains the search keys plus every column needed for filtering and output, either as key columns or included payload. That resembles a narrow projection of the table, but it is not a full row copy: engine metadata, visibility information, and nonincluded fields remain elsewhere. Avoiding table-page fetches is the main speed benefit.
How can an index-only scan still perform heap fetches in PostgreSQL? If all requested values are present in the index, I would expect the table to be irrelevant for that execution.

PostgreSQL must also determine whether each tuple is visible to the current transaction. B-tree entries do not carry all MVCC visibility facts, so the executor consults the heap unless the visibility map says the entire heap page is all-visible. Vacuuming and a mostly stable table increase that coverage; frequent updates can reduce it and reintroduce heap fetches.
Does INCLUDE behave differently from putting those output columns at the end of the indexed key? Both arrangements seem to cover the query, so I am unsure when the distinction changes speed.

Both can cover reads, but included columns are payload rather than part of the search ordering. They generally cannot support predicates or ordering as key columns do, and uniqueness applies only to the key portion. INCLUDE communicates intent and may allow more suitable storage behavior, though either choice enlarges entries and increases maintenance work.
When can a covering index become slower than the narrower index it replaces? Is the issue mainly that more columns make the B-tree deeper, or do cache effects matter sooner?

Cache effects often matter before an extra tree level appears. Wider entries mean fewer entries per page, more pages to scan, a larger working set, and more bytes written during updates. Large included values can also hit entry-size limits. A covering index pays off when avoided table reads are frequent enough to outweigh that footprint and write amplification.
How would I verify that the covering part is helping rather than just seeing an Index Only Scan label? Should I compare heap fetches and buffer reads across repeated executions?

Yes. Use an execution plan with actual timing and buffer statistics, then inspect heap fetches, shared-buffer hits and reads, rows processed, and total time. Test both warm and cold-ish cache conditions if they matter operationally. Also compare write cost and index size, because a faster isolated read may still be a poor workload-level trade.
If two queries need different payload columns but share the same search keys, when does one wide covering index make more sense than two narrower covering indexes?

One wide index avoids duplicating the key structure and may serve both queries, but every scan and update carries its larger payload. Two narrow indexes can preserve cache efficiency for each read while duplicating maintenance and key storage. Compare query frequency and overlap: a shared wide index favors balanced, frequent reads; separate indexes favor sharply different hot paths.
Why can an index on a boolean column be ignored even when the query filters on that column exactly? Since there are only two branches, I thought the lookup would be especially direct.

The tree lookup is direct, but finding the leaf range is only a small part of the work. If half the table matches, the engine may follow a huge number of row references and touch most table pages. A sequential scan can read those pages once with less overhead. Low cardinality is not inherently bad; match fraction and row layout matter.
How does a bitmap index scan improve that situation? I understand it collects row locations first, but does that make a low-selectivity index selective after the fact?

It does not change selectivity. It reorganizes the access: the engine gathers matching tuple locations into a bitmap, orders work by table page, and then visits each needed page efficiently. It can also combine bitmaps from several indexes with AND or OR. That reduces random page visits, though very broad matches still favor a sequential scan.
When would separate indexes on active and region combine better than one composite index on both? The bitmap approach sounds like it can assemble the composite key during the query.

Bitmap combination offers flexibility across many predicate combinations, but it does not recreate all advantages of a composite index. A composite key can jump directly to a narrower contiguous range and may supply ordering or coverage. Separate indexes are attractive when queries use each column independently; the composite usually wins for a frequent conjunction with meaningful selectivity.
Would a partial index containing only active rows usually be the cleaner option when inactive rows dominate, or does the boolean still remain too repetitive inside that smaller structure?

A partial index that stores only active rows can be excellent when active rows are a small, frequently queried subset. The boolean need not be a key at all; index another useful column and define the predicate as WHERE active. The index stays compact, but only queries whose conditions imply that predicate can use it reliably.
How much query speed should be traded for index maintenance on an update-heavy table? I know each relevant write changes the index, but I am unclear whether the tree is partly rebuilt each time.

Normal writes modify only affected paths and pages; they do not rebuild the whole tree. An insert finds a leaf and adds an entry, occasionally splitting a full page. Updates change indexes whose stored columns or row references require it, and deletes leave cleanup work. The cumulative costs are extra CPU, logging, page writes, cache pressure, and sometimes fragmentation.
When does a page split become noticeable to readers? Is it mainly a brief write delay, or can the split leave the index less sequential for later range scans?

A split can briefly add write latency and contention, but its longer effect is additional pages and potentially poorer physical locality. Logical key order remains correct, so range scans still work, yet adjacent logical pages may be less adjacent on storage. Repeated random inserts can lower page density and expand the index, increasing cache misses and scan I/O.
How does fill factor reduce that cost? I have seen it described as reserving empty space, though that sounds like deliberately making every index scan read more pages.

A lower fill factor leaves room on pages during index creation or rebuild, giving future inserts space before splits are needed. The tradeoff is exactly what you identified: the initial index is larger and scans may touch more pages. It helps most for indexes receiving inserts throughout the key space, not append-only keys that naturally grow at one edge.
For an increasing timestamp key, does the rightmost page become a hot page even though splits happen predictably? How does that affect concurrent insert speed compared with random UUID keys?

Increasing keys concentrate inserts at the right edge, which preserves locality but can create latch contention on the newest pages at high concurrency. Random UUIDs distribute insertion points and contention, yet cause more scattered writes, mid-tree splits, and a larger cache footprint. Which is faster depends on whether the workload is limited by contention or by memory and I/O efficiency.
When an indexed column is updated, can the database leave the index entry alone if the new value sorts onto the same leaf page, or must it always replace it?

Conceptually the old key-version relationship must be retired and a new one represented; merely landing on the same leaf does not make the update free. Exact mechanics vary by engine. PostgreSQL can avoid changing indexes during a HOT update only when no indexed column changes and page conditions allow it. Changing an indexed value prevents that optimization.
How do I tell whether read gains justify those costs without benchmarking every possible index combination? Are write latency and index hit counts enough to guide removal?

They are useful but incomplete. Combine query statistics, execution plans, index usage counters, write latency, index size, and representative load tests. Usage counts can miss rare but critical queries and do not show whether an index materially improved them. Evaluate candidates over a normal business cycle, account for constraints, then remove cautiously with a reversible deployment plan.
When is rebuilding or reindexing justified rather than letting ordinary cleanup handle fragmentation? I assume a large index with many deleted entries eventually loses its balanced shape.

B-trees generally remain height-balanced despite deletions; the problem is wasted space, excess pages, or corrupted structures, not an unbalanced shape. Routine vacuuming or background cleanup may reclaim reusable space without shrinking the file. Rebuild when measured bloat, degraded cache behavior, or maintenance guidance warrants the locking, I/O, temporary storage, and replication cost.
Why does wrapping an indexed column in a function often prevent the index from being used? If lower(email) is deterministic, it seems the optimizer could work backward to the original email values.

A normal index is ordered by the stored email values, not by their lowercase results. Many different original strings can map to one lowercase value, so there is no simple boundary to seek in the original ordering. Optimizers apply some safe rewrites, but generally you need an expression index on lower(email), a case-insensitive type, or a suitable collation.
How does that differ from applying a cast in the predicate? I sometimes see an index survive a cast and other times a harmless-looking conversion turns into a full scan.

It depends on which side is converted and whether the conversion preserves the index's ordering semantics. Casting a constant to the column type is often safe. Casting every column value may require computing a new value and can destroy the searchable ordering. Implicit casts, collations, precision changes, and engine-specific operator classes all affect whether a matching index condition exists.
When does rewriting a date expression into a range make it sargable? For example, is extracting the year equivalent to using two timestamp boundaries in every case?

A half-open range such as timestamp >= start and timestamp < next_start usually lets a timestamp index seek directly. It is equivalent to extracting a calendar year only when timezone, data type, and calendar semantics match. Boundary construction must use the intended timezone, especially for timestamp-with-time-zone values, or rows near year transitions may differ.
Would an expression index be preferable when many queries already use the function, or should the queries still be rewritten so the base index remains more generally useful?

Use an expression index when the transformed value is a stable, recurring access key and rewriting would be awkward or semantically different. Retain range-style predicates when they naturally fit the base ordering and serve more query shapes. An expression index adds storage and write computation, and queries usually must match the indexed expression closely enough for the optimizer to recognize it.
How can I distinguish a nonsargable predicate from an optimizer estimate that simply chooses not to use a valid index? Both appear as a sequential scan in the plan.

Inspect the plan's conditions and test a semantically equivalent index-friendly rewrite. If the expression appears only as a filter, the engine may lack an indexable condition. Check available operator classes and data types as well. Temporarily discouraging sequential scans can reveal whether an index path exists, but it should diagnose possibilities, not serve as the production fix.
How does a B-tree help with LIKE searches on text? I understand a fixed prefix can follow alphabetical order, but I am unsure where pattern matching stops behaving like a range.

A pattern such as 'data%' defines a contiguous lexical interval, so the engine can often seek to the prefix and scan until values no longer share it. A leading wildcard such as '%data' has no known starting boundary and usually cannot use ordinary B-tree ordering. Collation and operator-class details can also determine whether prefix optimization is valid.
When does an underscore wildcard still permit an index range? A pattern like ab_cd has a stable beginning, although the rest is not one continuous literal prefix.

The engine can use the literal prefix before the first wildcard, here 'ab', to form a broad index range. It then evaluates the full pattern as a residual filter. The underscore does not usually create separate precise seeks for every possible character, so usefulness depends on how selective that initial literal prefix is.
How exactly are trigram indexes different from storing many short prefixes? I tend to think of them as a B-tree broken into overlapping three-character keys.

A trigram index records associations between three-character fragments and rows, commonly through an inverted structure such as GIN or a signature-based GiST index. It is not a B-tree partitioned by prefix. Because fragments occur throughout a string, the index can propose candidates for contains and similarity searches; the full predicate may still recheck those candidates.
When would full-text search be a better index than trigrams for query speed? Both seem able to find words inside longer text without scanning every row.

Full-text indexes are better when searches concern language tokens, stemming, stop words, phrase logic, and relevance. Trigrams suit substring matching, misspellings, identifiers, and partial tokens. Full-text search may not find arbitrary character fragments, while trigram indexes can be larger and less semantically precise. Choose based on the query meaning, not only the shared avoidance of table scans.
When a join is slow, how does indexing the foreign-key column change the join strategy? I thought declaring the foreign key normally creates the needed lookup index automatically.

An index on the referencing column can make lookups from a parent row into matching child rows cheap and can accelerate parent updates or deletes that check references. Automatic creation varies by database: many systems index the referenced primary or unique key but do not automatically index the child foreign-key column. The join direction and chosen algorithm determine whether it helps.
How does a nested-loop join decide which side needs the index? Is the outer relation scanned once while the inner index is reopened for every outer row?

That is the usual model: produce rows from the outer input, then probe the inner access path for each relevant key. The index belongs on the inner join key. The engine may batch, cache, or memoize repeated probes, so reopened does not necessarily mean fresh physical I/O. Nested loops work best with few outer rows and cheap, selective probes.
When would the optimizer prefer a hash join even though both join columns are indexed? Does that indicate the indexes are ineffective, or only that too many rows participate?

Usually it means bulk processing is estimated cheaper. A hash join can scan each input once, build a hash table from the smaller side, and match many rows without repeated tree traversals. Indexes may remain valuable for other queries. Large participating fractions, weak filtering, poor clustering, and sufficient memory all make a hash join attractive.
How does a composite child index on parent_id and created_at help if the join only uses parent_id but the query later filters recent rows? Is the second key applied during the join?

If the query supplies both a parent_id equality and a created_at range, the composite index can make each inner probe reach only recent child entries. In that sense both conditions participate in the access path. If the date condition cannot be pushed into the scan, the index can still find the parent range, with date applied afterward as a filter.
When can mismatched data types on join keys block that indexed probe? The values may compare correctly after conversion, so I am unsure why storage type should affect the plan.

An implicit conversion may be applied to every value on the indexed side, turning the join expression into something that does not match the index ordering or operator class. It can also distort estimates. Some compatible conversions remain indexable, but matching key types is safer for performance and integrity. Inspect the plan for casts on the indexed column.
How would I index a three-table join without creating one index for the entire join path? I assume indexes can only organize columns from their own table.

Correct: a conventional index belongs to one table. Index the local join and filter keys that support useful access paths at each step, rather than trying to encode the whole path. The optimizer composes scans and joins across tables. Materialized views or denormalized tables can precompute cross-table relationships, but they introduce refresh and consistency costs.
How can an index remove the cost of ORDER BY rather than merely make the sort faster? If rows are stored separately from the index, I would expect them to lose the index order during fetching.

An ordered index scan emits row references in key order, and fetching the corresponding rows does not change that logical sequence. The reads may be physically scattered, but the executor returns rows in scan order. If the index ordering matches the requested columns, directions, and null handling, the database can avoid a separate sort operator entirely.
When does LIMIT make that ordered scan especially valuable? Is the database able to stop after ten entries even if a WHERE condition rejects some of the fetched rows?

LIMIT is valuable because the scan can stop once it has produced enough qualifying rows. If the WHERE condition is represented in the index, that may require only about ten entries. If it is a residual filter, the engine must continue past rejected entries, possibly scanning far more than ten. Data distribution determines how quickly acceptable rows appear.
How does mixed ordering work for an index like score descending and created_at ascending? Can a normal ascending composite index be scanned backward to satisfy both directions?

Scanning a composite index backward reverses every key direction together. An index on score ascending, created_at ascending can provide both ascending/ascending and descending/descending, but not descending/ascending. For that mixed request, define matching per-column directions if the engine supports them, or accept a sort for part or all of the result.
When would the optimizer choose a sort anyway despite a matching index? I assume avoiding the sort should always win for a large result set.

A matching index may require many random table fetches, while a sequential scan plus sort reads the table efficiently and sorts in memory or batches. For a large fraction of rows, that can be cheaper. A covering or well-clustered index strengthens the ordered path. Memory limits, row width, parallelism, and LIMIT also shift the choice.
How does keyset pagination benefit from the same index compared with OFFSET pagination? Both eventually need the next ordered group, but keyset seems to remember a position more directly.

Keyset pagination turns the last seen sort key into a range boundary, allowing the next request to seek near that position and read only the next page. OFFSET typically scans or produces the skipped rows before discarding them. Use a unique tie-breaker in both the ORDER BY and boundary predicate so pagination remains deterministic when primary sort values repeat.
What makes an optimizer misjudge whether an index will be faster? I read estimated rows as the database's sample count, but the value sometimes differs greatly from the actual rows.

Estimated rows are a prediction derived from statistics, not the size of a sample returned for that query. Statistics commonly summarize distinct counts, null fractions, frequent values, and value distributions. Estimates drift when data changes, samples miss skew, predicates are correlated, or expressions lack statistics. A wrong row estimate can make either index access or sequential scanning appear artificially cheap.
How does running ANALYZE correct the estimate? Does it scan enough index entries to learn selectivity, or does it inspect the underlying table independently of each index?

Typically ANALYZE samples table rows and builds column statistics that the planner can apply across access paths. It is not merely timing or counting entries in each index. Some engines also maintain index-specific statistics. The sample is approximate, so increasing the statistics target can improve detail for skewed columns at the cost of analysis time and catalog space.
When do single-column statistics fail for a composite index? If country and postal_code are both measured accurately, I would expect combining their selectivities to approximate the pair.

That approximation fails when the columns are dependent. Postal codes strongly imply countries, so multiplying independent selectivities may predict far too few rows. Multicolumn or extended statistics can record dependencies, joint distinct counts, or common combinations. They improve cardinality estimates, although they do not themselves provide the ordered access path that a composite index supplies.
How does stale cardinality lead specifically to a slow index plan? I usually associate missing an index with slowness, rather than choosing one too confidently.

If the planner expects a few matches but actually gets hundreds of thousands, it may choose repeated index probes, nested loops, or scattered heap reads. Those strategies have low startup cost but scale poorly with rows. A scan or hash join would have been cheaper at the true cardinality. Index use is an access decision, not automatically evidence of a good plan.
When I see cost values in EXPLAIN, should I compare them with milliseconds to judge how wrong the planner was? The totals often resemble no measured duration I can find.

Planner cost is an internal unit, not elapsed milliseconds. It combines modeled CPU and I/O work using configurable weights so candidate plans can be ranked. Compare estimated cost across alternatives within the same configuration, then use actual timing and buffer data for observed performance. A cost-to-time relationship may be roughly correlated, but it is not a direct conversion.
How can histogram boundaries make a range predicate inaccurate when the column is highly skewed? I assume values between two boundaries are treated as evenly distributed.

That is often the approximation for values not captured separately as frequent values. If a narrow interval contains a local cluster hidden inside a broad histogram bucket, uniform interpolation can miss badly. Larger statistics targets, most-common-value lists, specialized statistics, or partitioning may help. Rapidly changing distributions also require timely analysis to keep those summaries representative.
When does forcing an index help diagnose this without becoming a permanent hint? I want to separate a bad estimate from an index that is genuinely slower under current caching.

Use a session-local planner setting or engine-specific hint only as an experiment, then collect actual rows, time, and buffer activity for both paths under comparable conditions. If the forced path wins while estimates were far off, investigate statistics. If it loses despite corrected cardinality, the cost model or physical access pattern may already favor the scan.
How do I account for cache state while comparing those plans? Repeating each query warms different pages, so the second execution seems biased toward whichever index was just tested.

Measure the operating condition you actually care about, often a naturally warm shared cache under mixed load. Alternate test order, run multiple samples, record buffer hits versus reads, and avoid treating one cold run as definitive. Truly cold tests may require environment-level cache control, which is disruptive; a staging workload or replay is usually safer and more representative.
How does clustering a table by an index improve range-query speed? I understand it places nearby keys together, but I am unsure whether the index then owns the physical row order permanently.

Clustering arranges table rows to resemble an index's key order, so a range scan can fetch fewer, more sequential table pages. In systems where clustering is a one-time rewrite, the index does not permanently control later placement; inserts and updates gradually weaken the correlation. Some storage engines organize the table around a clustered primary index continuously, with different tradeoffs.
When does correlation become poor enough that the optimizer changes to a sequential scan? Is there a measurable threshold, or is it folded into the random-page cost estimate?

It is folded into the estimated page-fetch cost along with selectivity, table size, caching assumptions, and cost parameters. There is no universal correlation threshold. PostgreSQL records a correlation statistic that helps estimate whether heap access will be sequential or scattered. The plan changes when the total modeled cost crosses that of alternatives, not at one fixed value.
How would this interact with two important range indexes, such as created_at and account_id? The table can only be physically ordered for one of them at a time.

Exactly. Choose physical locality for the access pattern with the greatest benefit, often large range scans or the dominant write pattern. The other index remains logically ordered but may perform scattered table reads. Partitioning, covering indexes, or materialized projections can provide alternative locality, though each adds operational or storage cost rather than giving one table two physical orders.
When are random heap reads mostly avoided because the operating system reads ahead? I wonder whether clustering matters less on SSD storage than the cost model suggests.

Read-ahead helps when requested pages form predictable sequences, which is precisely what good correlation creates. SSDs narrow the latency gap between random and sequential I/O, and a large cache narrows it further, but scattered access still causes more operations and poorer locality. Calibrate cost settings and benchmark representative concurrency rather than assuming the storage medium removes the effect.
When does a prepared statement stop choosing the best index for its actual parameter value? I have heard that caching the plan can freeze selectivity from the first execution.

Behavior varies by engine. Some systems compile using an early parameter value and reuse that plan; others compare custom parameter-aware plans with a generic plan after several executions. The first value is not always literally frozen, but parameter distribution can still make one reusable plan poor for certain values. This is commonly called parameter sniffing or parameter sensitivity.
How can the same equality predicate need different access paths? If both values use the same indexed column, I would expect the B-tree work to differ only in result count.

Result count is enough to change the best path. A rare value may justify an index seek plus a handful of table fetches, while a common value may make a scan cheaper. That choice can also affect join order and join algorithm, magnifying the difference. The B-tree traversal stays cheap; processing the matching rows does not.
When would a generic plan intentionally ignore a useful index? Is it averaging selectivity across all parameter values, or estimating an unknown value through another fallback rule?

A generic plan estimates without the concrete parameter and typically uses column statistics plus an engine-specific unknown-value rule. That may resemble average selectivity, but it is not always a literal average. If the estimated typical match is broad, the generic plan may choose a scan even though an index would be excellent for rare values.
How do I confirm that plan reuse is the cause rather than ordinary cache variation? The slow cases appear for common keys, but their pages might also be less resident.

Capture actual plans for representative rare and common parameters, including row estimates, buffer activity, and whether the plan is generic or custom. Compare prepared execution with an equivalent statement compiled using the literal value. If estimates and access paths change consistently by compilation mode while buffers explain little, parameter sensitivity is the stronger diagnosis.
When is recompiling each execution a reasonable fix? It seems to restore the right index choice, although planning itself adds latency and CPU under concurrency.

Recompilation is reasonable for expensive, infrequent queries whose optimal plans vary substantially by parameter. It is less attractive for tiny, high-throughput statements where planning can rival execution cost. Alternatives include separate query forms for value classes, updated statistics, filtered indexes, engine-specific adaptive features, or accepting a robust plan that is not optimal for every value.
How can a partial index help with parameter-sensitive values if the prepared predicate uses a placeholder? I assume the planner cannot prove the placeholder belongs to the indexed subset.

That is a common limitation for generic planning. To use a partial index, the planner must prove the query predicate implies the index predicate. An unconstrained placeholder usually cannot establish that for every execution. A custom plan may succeed after seeing the value, or the application can use a distinct statement whose fixed predicate explicitly matches the subset.
How do overlapping indexes affect query planning and speed? An index on account_id seems contained inside one on account_id and created_at, so I would expect the shorter index to be unnecessary.

The composite index can support account_id lookups through its leading key, making the shorter index logically redundant for many predicates. Yet the single-column index is narrower, may fit better in cache, scan fewer pages, and cost less to probe. Whether that difference matters depends on workload and payload. Redundancy should be measured, not inferred only from key containment.
When does keeping both make the optimizer slower just from having more choices? Could plan enumeration become significant before the extra write and storage costs do?

A few overlapping indexes rarely make planning the dominant cost, but dozens can enlarge the search space, consume metadata cache, and create unstable near-equivalent choices. Write amplification and memory footprint usually hurt sooner. Planning effects become more visible in complex joins or partitioned schemas, where each additional access path participates in a much larger combination of possibilities.
How can I identify a truly redundant index when uniqueness, included columns, sort direction, and partial predicates differ? Usage counters alone seem to merge several meanings of usefulness.

Compare full definitions and responsibilities, not just leading columns. Check uniqueness and constraint backing, key order and direction, operator classes, predicates, included columns, and validity. Then map each index to observed plans and important query shapes. An unused index may still enforce a constraint or serve rare operational work, while two used indexes may nevertheless be consolidatable.
When combining two indexes into one wider index, how should I account for queries that only scan the shared prefix? I assume wider leaf entries reduce their speed somewhat.

Yes, prefix-only queries may read a larger tree and fewer entries per page. Quantify the change using index size, tree height, buffer reads, and latency for those scans. Consolidation saves write and storage cost but can tax the hottest simple lookup. A wide replacement is most convincing when suffix columns also eliminate table reads or sorting often enough.
How long should index usage be observed before removal? Some monthly queries may be absent from a short sample, but indefinite monitoring leaves every questionable index in place.

Observe at least one complete workload cycle that includes reporting, maintenance, and peak events, and preserve query-history evidence across restarts if counters reset. Review application code and constraint dependencies too. For uncertain cases, make the index invisible where supported or remove it through a reversible change, monitor regressions, and retain a tested recreation plan.

Why does a partial index sometimes remain unused even when the query's WHERE clause looks stricter than the index predicate? I assumed filtering happens first and then the smaller index is considered.

The planner chooses an access path before execution, so it must prove from the query expression that every qualifying row belongs to the partial index. It relies on recognizable logical implication, not on observing rows after filtering. Equivalent-looking casts, functions, parameter placeholders, or differently structured conditions can prevent proof even when a person sees the relationship.
How exact must that implication be? If the index covers orders where status equals open, should a query for open orders from this month always qualify for it?

Yes, when the query explicitly includes status = open, the additional date restriction makes it stricter and normally preserves implication. The partial index keys must still support a useful scan; eligibility alone does not guarantee selection. If status is hidden behind a function, supplied through a generic parameter, or represented inconsistently, proof may fail depending on the engine.
When does putting the predicate column into the index key add value? Since every stored row has status open, indexing status itself seems like repeating a constant.

Usually it adds little search value because the predicate already guarantees that constant. Keys should instead support filters, joins, or ordering within the open subset. Include status only if coverage rules require the value for an index-only query or an engine has a specific limitation. Omitting it keeps entries narrower and makes the design's purpose clearer.
How does a partial unique index enforce uniqueness? Does it allow the same value outside the predicate while treating rows inside it as one separate key space?

Exactly. Only rows satisfying the predicate contribute entries, so uniqueness is enforced among that subset. Rows outside it can repeat the indexed value because they have no entry in that index. This is useful for rules such as one active record per account, provided the predicate precisely represents the intended business condition and handles nulls correctly.
When can the subset grow enough that the partial index loses its speed advantage? Is there a point where it behaves no differently from a full index with the same keys?

Its advantage fades as the subset approaches the full table because size, cache footprint, and maintenance approach those of a full index. It can still omit irrelevant entries and encode useful uniqueness, so the difference is not binary. Track predicate prevalence, index size, and plan behavior; a condition that began rare may cease being selective as application state changes.
How should queries be written when status can be open or pending and the index predicate includes both? Would using IN match more reliably than two OR conditions?

Use a consistent canonical expression when practical, because planner theorem proving is intentionally limited. Many engines normalize IN and simple OR forms, but casts, null semantics, and parameters can still matter. Verify with plans rather than assuming equivalence recognition. If the condition is central, encapsulating it in generated data or a stable schema convention can reduce expression drift.
When would separate partial indexes for open and pending be faster than one partial index covering both states? The queries often request only one state at a time.

Separate indexes can be smaller and more selective for single-state queries, especially if each has different useful key order or payload. One combined index reduces duplicated structure and write paths and can serve queries spanning both states. Compare state frequencies and query patterns; if status is not a key in the combined index, single-state scans may inspect both subsets.
When does a BRIN index make a large time-series query faster than a B-tree? I understand it stores one pointer per page range, so it seems much less exact.

BRIN stores summaries, such as minimum and maximum values, for groups of table pages rather than one pointer per range. A timestamp condition lets it skip page ranges whose summaries cannot match, then recheck rows in candidate ranges. It works well when timestamp values correlate with physical insertion order, producing a tiny index with low maintenance cost.
How does the pages-per-range setting change query speed? Smaller ranges should reject irrelevant pages more precisely, but I assume the summary index grows toward a regular B-tree.

Smaller ranges improve pruning precision and reduce false-positive heap reads, while creating more summary tuples and maintenance work. The index grows, but it remains summary-based and usually far smaller than a B-tree because it still lacks one entry per row. The best setting balances correlation, common query-window size, table scale, and acceptable recheck I/O.
When out-of-order events are inserted, does BRIN become fragmented in the same sense as a B-tree, or do the minimum and maximum summaries simply become wider?

The main problem is wider or overlapping summaries, not B-tree-style page fragmentation. A late timestamp placed in a recent physical page range expands that range's minimum and maximum, causing more ranges to survive future pruning. Occasional disorder may be harmless; sustained disorder weakens correlation enough that BRIN returns too many candidate pages to help much.
How would I choose between BRIN and table partitioning by month? Both seem to skip old data, although partitioning acts before individual indexes are scanned.

Partitioning provides coarse structural pruning plus lifecycle benefits such as dropping or archiving whole months, but it adds routing, metadata, and operational complexity. BRIN is simpler and can prune page ranges within one table. They are complementary: monthly partitions can each use BRIN for narrower time windows, or B-trees where highly selective lookups justify their cost.
